claims.text: Pre-exposure annealing of Q235 steel promotes formation of a continuous iron-oxide scale.
The annealing-induced oxide scale is adherent to Q235 steel.
The annealing-induced oxide scale consists mainly of Fe3O4.
A continuous, adherent Fe3O4-rich scale resists aggressive salt-driven oxidation at high temperature.
Annealing Q235 steel before salt exposure slows degradation relative to the as-received state.
As-received Q235 steel has a native oxide layer and a typical microstructure.
Annealing in ambient air at approximately 800 °C for 1 hour is proposed to form and stabilize a protective oxide scale.
The Fe-oxide scale acts as a barrier to aggressive-ion and oxygen ingress during hot corrosion.
A non-continuous or absent protective scale permits faster oxidation under salt attack.
Salt attack accelerates scale spallation when the protective scale is absent or non-continuous.
After identical 800 °C salt exposure, annealed Q235 steel will exhibit less mass change than untreated Q235 steel.
After identical 800 °C salt exposure, annealed Q235 steel will exhibit a smoother and more intact oxide scale than untreated Q235 steel.
After identical 800 °C salt exposure, annealed Q235 steel will exhibit lower corrosion-induced degradation indicators than untreated Q235 steel.
The proposed protective mechanism applies mainly to hot-corrosion conditions in the 700–900 °C range.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at lower temperatures because oxidation kinetics are slower.
The proposed mechanism may not govern degradation when mechanical abrasion or other degradation mechanisms dominate.
Minor alloying and processing-history variations in Q235 steel may alter oxide-scale composition and adherence.
The presence of V2O5 in the salt can affect oxide-scale stability and protective behavior.
